title: The Tourist Questions Behind Every Five-Star Review
seoTitle: The Tourist Questions Behind Every Five-Star Review
excerpt: A Nizwa front desk wrote down every visitor question for two weeks. The one question nobody bothered to record turned out to be behind most of the hotel's five-star reviews.
seoDescription: The tourist questions hotel desks and tour lines hear every day, what they reveal, what repeat answers cost, and the tiny reply that earns five-star reviews.
topic: What Tourists Ask, According to Everyone Who Serves Them

blocks.text: For two weeks this October, Shamsa asked her front desk team in Nizwa to write down every question a visitor asked, on the phone or across the counter. Most of the list was predictable. One question, the one nobody thought worth recording, turned out to sit behind most of the hotel's five-star reviews, and answering it well costs almost nothing.

segments.text: Shamsa is a composite character, built from the front office managers who run hotel desks across the interior. Her hotel has 120 rooms, six front office agents, a switchboard that passes to the night auditor after 11 pm, and an old phone menu offering reservations, the restaurant and "all other enquiries". If you run a hotel desk, a tour line or a car hire counter, her tally sheet probably looks a lot like yours.

blocks.text: A tally sheet on the counter

segments.text: The idea started on a slow Tuesday. Shamsa taped a sheet beside every phone: one line per question, and a tick each time it came back. The night auditor got a sheet too, because October calls ignore shift times. In October, a couple in Munich finishing dinner at 9 pm are calling Nizwa at 11 pm, when the desk is down to one person.
Those callers matter. In the first half of 2026, Europeans were the largest group of international guests in the country's three- to five-star hotels, at 246,603, with Asian guests next at 162,978,
according to national statistics reported in August
. Most ask in English, many in German, French or Italian, and plenty
switch languages halfway through a call

blocks.text: The tourist questions that kept coming back

segments.text: After 14 days the sheets held just over 1,900 ticks. Twelve questions made up roughly six in ten of them. Shamsa compared notes with a tour operator's call desk in Muscat and the airport car hire counter that sends guests up the road to her. Their lists matched hers almost line for line. Here are the most common ones.

blocks.caption: Composite tally from a hotel desk, a tour line and a car hire counter

Night calls

segments.text: Look at the right-hand column again. Almost none of these questions is about the hotel. They are about the unfamiliar day ahead: the road, the dress code, the money, the manners. A visitor calling at 11 pm about the goat market isn't really asking for a time. They want someone local to tell them it will be fine.

blocks.text: Tourists rarely call about the room; they call to find out whether they will be all right out there.

segments.text: This is where the phone menu lets them down. None of these questions fits "reservations" or "restaurant", so they all land in "other enquiries". That option rings the same busy counter where a family is checking in. At night it rings the auditor, who is closing the day's accounts. Some callers hang up, and a few book somewhere else. What finally fixed Shamsa's nights comes later, and it was not more staff.

blocks.text: What the same twelve answers cost

segments.text: The repeat answers cost real money. But the unanswered night calls cost nearly seven times as much. Shamsa stopped asking "how do we answer faster?" and started asking "how do we stop leaving a visitor unanswered?"

Next, Shamsa read 60 recent five-star reviews alongside the tally. The reviews rarely praised the room. They named people and quoted advice: "Khalfan told us to leave at 7 for the market." "The night desk sent us the route up the mountain and a list of what to bring."

That was the missing question. At the end of many calls, visitors had asked, "Can you write that down for me?" Nobody ticked it, because it didn't feel like a question about Oman. Yet the guests who got the answer on their phone, with a map pin and a time, were the ones who came back to write the review.

blocks.text: The answer that earns five stars is rarely the cleverest one; it is the one the guest can still read on their phone the next morning.

blocks.quote: Nobody writes a review about the room key. They write about the person who told them to leave early for the goat market.

blocks.text: How Shamsa's desk turned questions into reviews

items.text: The twelve answers are written once, in agreed words, in English and Arabic, and the shift lead checks them every Sunday. Now the night auditor and the day team give the same answer.
Any answer that includes a time, a place or a price goes to the guest's phone straight after the call, with a map pin.
The top five answers now go into the pre-arrival message sent three days before check-in. That means fewer calls and calmer arrivals.
A line that never rings out.

For nights and the Friday morning rush, the hotel replaced its phone menu with an AI voice agent, software that holds a natural spoken conversation on the phone line. It answers the twelve questions in the caller's language, takes packed breakfast requests and leaves anything unusual as a note for the morning shift.
Complaints, anniversaries and guests who are lost or unwell still go straight to a person, day or night.

segments.text: By the end of the month, the unanswered night calls in her log were close to zero. Her agents got their afternoons back too. With fewer goat market calls, they had more time for the guest standing in front of them.
If you run a hotel desk, a tour operator's phone line or a rental counter, your visitors are asking the same dozen things this week. Find out which ones before the December peak arrives.

items.text: Count before you buy anything. Two weeks of tallies tells you more than any software demo.
Write each answer once, so every shift gives the same one.
Send the answer in writing. It takes your agent ten seconds, and it is the line guests quote back in reviews.
Cover the hours when visitors call, not just the hours your team works.

blocks.title: Try this today
paragraphs: Tape a sheet beside every phone and at the counter for 14 days. Write one line per question and add a tick each time it repeats.
Ask the night shift to tally too, and to note the time of each call.
At the end, circle your top twelve and check whether your phone menu has a button for any of them.
Then read your last 30 five-star reviews and underline every name and every tip guests quote back. That is your answer sheet.

items.q: Will tourists mind talking to an AI agent at night?
items.a: Most callers mind a phone that keeps ringing far more. Keep it honest: the agent should say what it is, answer the common questions well and pass anything personal to a person.

items.q: Which questions should always stay with staff?
items.a: Complaints, refunds, health or safety concerns and special occasions. These are calls where the caller needs to feel heard, not just informed.

items.q: Does this work for a tour operator, not just a hotel?
items.a: Yes. Tour lines get the same kinds of questions, plus pickup times and what to bring. The tally and the answer sheet work the same way.

segments.text: Tourists ask the same few questions because they share the same few worries. Give the same answer every time, send it in writing, and make sure someone (or something) picks up at 11 pm. That is most of a five-star review, and very little of it costs extra.
